title: How Congress might take back its trade powers and limit Trump's tariffs
gist: After Democrats won both chambers in the November 2026 midterms, PIIE's Inu Manak argues Congress should reclaim delegated trade authority by closing loopholes in Section 232 and Section 301, through approval/disapproval resolutions, narrower executive discretion, transparency and scope limits. She expects veto-proof majorities only for Canada-specific relief, so comprehensive reform is unlikely before the next president, and tariff uncertainty will persist.

themes.theme: Midterm backlash creates a tariff-reform mandate

insights.claim: The president's party suffered a stunning defeat in the November 2026 US midterm elections, which the author reads as voters rejecting unpopular policies including immigration enforcement, the war in Iran, and tariffs.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: The political cost of tariffs is now explicit, which raises the odds of tariff rollback pressure in 2027.
insights.quote: the accumulation of unpopular policies—including immigration enforcement, the war in Iran, and tariffs—was thoroughly rebuked
insights.locator: Americans are unhappy with the direction

insights.claim: An NBC News exit poll from 45 states in the 2026 midterms found 66 percent of voters thought President Trump's tariffs had hurt the US economy.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Broad anti-tariff sentiment gives legislators political cover to vote against tariffs, even members of the president's party.
insights.quote: 66 percent of voters thought President Donald Trump's tariffs had hurt the national economy
insights.locator: Congress may want to start with trade policy

insights.claim: Democrats will control both the House and Senate from January 2027 after spending billions of dollars on TV ads that portrayed tariffs negatively, and voters are likely to expect them to claw back tariffs as a way to lower consumer costs.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Tariff rollback is being framed as an affordability policy, so watch for votes tied to consumer-price relief.

insights.claim: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, on track to become House Speaker in January 2027, has said rolling back Trump's tariffs will be a top Democratic priority but has not said which tariffs or trade statutes will be targeted.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Which statutes are targeted is the key open question; watch Jeffries' agenda for specifics.

themes.theme: Sections 232 and 301 are the core tariff loopholes

insights.claim: Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 (national security sectoral tariffs) and Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 (which props up baseline tariffs of 10-12 percent on nearly all US imports) are the two statutes the president uses to avoid accountability on tariffs.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Durable tariff relief requires changes to these two statutes; rollbacks elsewhere leave the bulk of the tariff wall in place.
insights.quote: Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which is propping up baseline tariffs of 10-12 percent on nearly all US imports

insights.claim: Tariffs under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 (balance of payments, struck down by the US Court of International Trade but on appeal) and Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (used against Canada, also under court challenge) are low-hanging fruit for Congress, but repealing them would not reclaim the core delegated trade powers.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Court rulings or easy repeals of Section 122/338 tariffs should not be read as an end to the trade war; the sectoral and baseline tariffs remain.
insights.quote: tackling these measures will not go far enough in reclaiming trade authorities that Congress has delegated to the president

insights.claim: For Canada, Section 338 tariffs are less economically significant than the Section 232 sectoral tariffs, and US-Canada negotiations over the Section 232 tariffs broke down in August 2026.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Canadian trade exposure depends on Section 232 sectoral relief, not on the Section 338 court case.

insights.claim: Only comprehensive reform of Section 232 and Section 301, the two statutes that have kept trade wars going since 2018, would meaningfully reduce the uncertainty in US economic relations; anything less will do little.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Expect trade-policy uncertainty premia to persist unless core-statute reform passes, which the author thinks is unlikely this Congress.
insights.quote: Anything less will do little to reduce the uncertainty that has plagued US economic relations

themes.theme: Reform toolkit: votes, discretion, transparency, scope

insights.claim: A joint resolution of approval, which requires Congress to vote on a tariff before it takes effect, is a stronger check than a disapproval resolution, which forces Congress to repeal tariffs after the fact and is politically harder for the president's party.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Whether a bill uses an approval or a disapproval mechanism decides whether it actually constrains future tariffs.
insights.locator: The second, and more robust, option

insights.claim: The 2025 Trade Review Act by Senators Maria Cantwell and Chuck Grassley would cap new or increased tariffs at 60 days unless Congress passes a joint resolution of approval, and would let Congress end tariffs at any time by disapproval resolution; like other such bills, it would face a presidential veto that needs two-thirds of both houses to override.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: This bipartisan bill is the most likely template for reform; follow its cosponsors and vote counts.

insights.claim: Congress could narrow presidential discretion by moving Section 232 national-security investigations from the Secretary of Commerce to the Department of Defense, and Section 301 investigations from the politically appointed USTR to an independent agency such as the US International Trade Commission.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Moving investigations to agencies outside the president's control would make new sectoral tariffs harder to justify and easier to predict.
insights.locator: Another way to limit executive abuse

insights.claim: The second Trump administration has not published the Section 232 reports from the Commerce Secretary that underlie its tariff decisions, unlike the first-term autos report, which the Biden administration released. Requiring disclosure and stronger judicial review would make these tariffs easier to challenge.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Stronger judicial review would expose sectoral tariffs to court challenges that national-security deference now blocks.
insights.quote: In the second Trump administration, these reports have not been made public

insights.claim: Tariff exclusions are granted opaquely: a 2023 GAO review found problems in the Section 232 exclusions process, including unneeded exclusions, and hundreds of products were exempted from Section 301 tariffs in the first Trump term through an opaque process even though the statute has no exclusion mechanism.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Exclusion rules decide which companies and sectors are exposed to tariffs; reform could formalize carve-outs for consumer products, energy, or trade-agreement partners.
insights.locator: How and why certain products are excluded

insights.claim: Congress could define national security narrowly, as the Toomey-Warner bill did, and exclude products with no obvious security use, such as kitchen cabinets or groceries, as well as defense-industrial-base countries and security allies, from national-security tariffs.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Scope limits would remove the legal basis for sectoral tariffs on consumer goods such as cabinets and groceries.
insights.quote: the protection of the United States from foreign aggression; and does not otherwise include the protection of the general welfare of the United States
insights.locator: Finally, Congress will need to weigh

insights.claim: Section 301 was designed as an investigation-driven tool to give the president leverage to lower foreign trade barriers in negotiations with a single country, not to raise US barriers, and Alan Wolff, the author of the original statute, has been skeptical of its use for tariffs aimed at forced labor.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: The gap between what Section 301 was meant to do and how it is used now gives reformers a strong argument and may weaken the legal case for the baseline tariffs.
insights.quote: Today, its application is far removed from that intent.
insights.locator: Such reforms should entail serious reflection

themes.theme: Allies, Canada and limits of exemptions

insights.claim: Trump's second-term trade war has targeted allies and adversaries alike, including Canada and free trade agreement partner South Korea, and Canadians are now more likely to see the US as an enemy or potential threat than as a friend.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Damage to alliances may outlast tariff relief and weigh on cross-border investment and cooperation.

insights.claim: Senator Christopher Coons' 2025 bill would limit tariffs on NATO members, major non-NATO allies and US FTA partners, but allies may need more than targeted exemptions to trust the US again after Congress-approved FTAs and multilateral rules were violated, and Congress may keep some ally tariffs as leverage for concessions.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Do not expect blanket relief for allies; partial exemptions with leverage retained are more likely.
insights.quote: allies may need more than targeted tariff exemptions to restore trust in the US

insights.claim: A veto-proof majority may exist for Canada-specific tariff relief but probably not for broader tariff reform, so the incoming Congress is unlikely to achieve comprehensive reform because of internal party pressure and lobbying for continued protection.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Canada-specific relief is the most plausible legislative tariff change in 2027-28; the broad baseline and sectoral tariffs probably stay.
insights.quote: That may exist for Canada-specific tariff relief but not for broader efforts.
insights.locator: Of course, for any legislative action

insights.claim: Congress may hold tariff votes even if the bills are unlikely to pass, to put members on record before the next election and to lay groundwork for the next president and Congress to restore checks and balances on trade.
insights.speaker: Inu Manak
insights.so_what: Tariff votes in 2027-28 will signal where each member stands and shape the 2028 trade agenda more than they change tariffs.
insights.locator: Of course, for any legislative action
